deep.reconstruction:
The page has no handwritten text. It holds only pencil figures, drawn on the back of a 1982 IBM JES2 printout banner page; the paper is reused and has nothing to do with the mathematics. The previous page (66) treats 'pantalons' (pairs of pants) subdivided in a standard way, with a set J of three boundary curves ('trans'). Each pair of pants carries weights alpha', beta', gamma' that count how often arcs meet each boundary curve. These are converted into arc counts alpha, beta, gamma by solving beta+gamma=alpha' and its permutations, which requires alpha'+beta'+gamma' to be even. Gluing data are bijections between Z/alpha-torsors of points on the boundary circles. The next page (68) shows a graph whose vertices are labelled 0, 1, infinity (a dessin / Belyi-type map), surrounded by nested level curves.

Page 67 sits between these and reads as a set of topological illustrations of the same set-up:
(1) An oval with one marked point: a disc or circle around a single puncture, the trivial or degenerate case.
(2) Two circled marked points joined by a thick segment, inside an elongated oval. A faint long curve runs through both points, and short strokes radiate from one endpoint. This is the standard picture of the simple closed curve that bounds a regular neighbourhood of an arc joining two punctures. Such curves are the building blocks of pants decompositions of punctured spheres (and of half-twists).
(3) A second, shorter copy of (2) inside a larger oval: the same configuration nested in a bigger region.
(4) A heavily retraced oval with six or seven marked points on its boundary and faint chords or radii. This most plausibly shows a boundary circle carrying alpha' marked points, i.e. the Z/alpha'-torsor of intersection points with the arc system that appears in the gluing condition of page 66.
(5) An oval containing two small discs joined by a double band, with radial arcs running from the discs to the outer boundary. This is a pair of pants (disc minus two discs) with its seams and a family of transverse arcs: the 'pantalon subdivisé de façon standard' with weighted arc families joining boundary components.
(6) Four small tick marks at the top, probably doodles or point markers.

Taken together, the page visualises encoding a weighted multicurve or arc system on a surface through a pants decomposition plus combinatorial gluing data. This is essentially Dehn–Thurston-type coordinates, in the combinatorial language of maps (cartes) that Grothendieck was developing.
errors: No mathematical statements on the page, so nothing to check. Readings of the sketches are interpretive.

deep.surprise_reason: These are pure illustration sketches with no text, accompanying standard pants-decomposition and arc-system combinatorics. The mathematics they serve (on the neighbouring pages) is close to Dehn–Thurston coordinates and is not new.
transcription_corrections: In sketch (2), a faint long curve passes through both circled points and extends past them, and short strokes radiate from the right endpoint. These are not mentioned in the transcription.
Sketch (4) is a heavily retraced double oval with about seven boundary points and faint interior chords or radii converging inward, not just 'arcs joining them'.
Sketch (5) shows two small discs joined by a double-line band inside the outer oval, with radial segments from each disc to the outer boundary; it looks like a pair of pants with seams.
